stdout: usage: bale retry [-h] [--sid SID] [--staging-dir STAGING_DIR] [--verbose]
[--no-interact] [--allow-out-of-scope PATH]
[--allow-missing-required-check NAME]
[--accept-checkpoint-change] [--accept-base-drift PATH]
[--no-sandbox] [--json]
tarball
Discard the HOLDed apply state for an open session — reset the bale/<sid>
branch, wipe the session's staging — and run the apply pipeline against a new
response tarball, keeping the session open so the new attempt lands in the
same session id. The target session is read from the tarball itself — its
manifest.responds_to — however many sessions are open (board 71; the same
resolution bare `bale apply` uses); it must name an open session. --sid, when
given, vets that resolution rather than picking: a --sid that disagrees with
the tarball refuses naming both. Every resolution refusal fires before any
HOLD state is touched. The tarball argument is resolved against
apply.search_paths in bale.toml the same way `bale apply` does.
A HOLD is retried on one of two rulings. When the work was wrong, the worker
ships a corrected response and `bale retry <new-tarball>` runs it. When the
blind checkpoint was wrong, the planner publishes an amendment, `bale amend-
checkpoint` commits it and prints the retry line, and the retry of the same
response takes the --accept-checkpoint-change rung: the provenance gate
refuses the changed oracle until that flag accepts it, per invocation.
The per-attempt flags mirror `bale apply`'s (--verbose, --no-interact,
--allow-out-of-scope, --allow-missing-required-check, --accept-checkpoint-
change, --accept-base-drift, --no-sandbox, --json), since retry reruns the
same pipeline. Apply's inspection flags (--show-validator, --show-apply-
script, --dry-run) are deliberately absent here: they read the tarball or the
open session without touching the HOLD state, so they work verbatim through
`bale apply` at any point, retry pending or not.
positional arguments:
tarball               Path to the new response-<sid>.tar.gz.
options:
-h, --help            show this help message and exit
--sid SID             Vetting only (board 71): the session is resolved from
the tarball's own manifest.responds_to, however many
sessions are open. When given, --sid must equal that
responds_to; a mismatch refuses naming both sids and
the tarball. Never required.
--staging-dir STAGING_DIR
Where to stage the apply (default:
<repo>/.bale/staging/<sid>, per open session). An
explicit path is resolved relative to cwd, is used
verbatim (no <sid> suffix), and is refused if it
already exists.
--verbose             Stream validation.sh output live to the terminal in
addition to the session log (BALE.md §8.5) — same
semantics as `bale apply --verbose` (retry reruns the
same pipeline). Without it, validation output goes to
.bale/logs/<sid>.log only and the walkthrough summary
carries the verdict.
--no-interact         Run without prompting — same semantics as `bale apply
--no-interact` (retry reruns the same pipeline):
walkthrough takes its default action, the post-apply
hook confirmation resolves from
apply.hook_auto_accept, and every bypassed prompt logs
its decision and source.
--allow-out-of-scope PATH
Admit one changes[] path that lies outside the
session's own declared scope, past the own-scope drift
gate (BALE.md §8.1 step 14, §11 row 22) — same
semantics as `bale apply --allow-out-of-scope`. Repeat
the flag per path; any out-of-scope path NOT named
still refuses. Per-invocation only — there is
deliberately no config key, and the override is never
carried forward from a failed apply attempt: a retry
that needs it re-states it. Every use is logged
prominently (FORCE: line in the session log) and the
admitted paths are stamped into the session's
telemetry record. On a TTY the refusal offers the same
admission as a per-path y/N (default decline;
v0.4.27), and prints a composed `bale retry` re-run
line carrying one flag per drifted path.
--allow-missing-required-check NAME
Admit one required check name past the required-check
superset gate (BALE.md §8.1 step 15, §11 row 26) —
same semantics as `bale apply --allow-missing-
required-check`. Repeat the flag per name; any missing
required name NOT named still refuses. Per-invocation
only — no config key, and the override is never
carried forward from a failed apply attempt: a retry
that needs it re-states it. Every effective use is
logged prominently (FORCE: line) and the admitted
names are stamped into the session's telemetry record.
--accept-checkpoint-change
Accept a blind checkpoint that changed between pack
and apply — same semantics as `bale apply --accept-
checkpoint-change` (retry reruns the same pipeline):
the current base-tree version runs, the use is FORCE-
logged, and the attempt's telemetry stamp records
stamp_matched: false. Per-invocation only — no config
key, and the override is never carried forward from a
failed apply attempt: a retry that needs it re-states
it.
--accept-base-drift PATH
Admit one changes[] path past the base-drift gate —
same semantics as `bale apply --accept-base-drift`
(retry reruns the same pipeline): the response's bytes
land over the moved base for exactly the named paths,
FORCE-logged and stamped into the attempt's
base_drift_overrides telemetry field. Repeat the flag
per path; any drifted path NOT named still refuses.
Per-invocation only — no config key, and the override
is never carried forward from a failed apply attempt:
a retry that needs it re-states it. Note the repack
alternative: a fresh `bale pack` restamps against the
current base by construction, so regenerating the
response against today's tree clears the drift without
any override.
--no-sandbox          Run the response scripts unconfined for this
invocation — same semantics as `bale apply --no-
sandbox` (retry reruns the same pipeline). Per-
invocation only: the bypass is never carried forward
from a failed apply attempt — a retry that needs it
re-states it — while bale.toml's project-layer
[sandbox] enabled = false (v0.4.26) is the durable
form retry inherits structurally, same config. Every
use of either is FORCE-logged in the session log. On a
TTY a refusing self-probe offers the same escape as a
y/N (v0.4.27; sandbox_off_source: prompt). `bale
revert` executes no response scripts and takes no such
flag.
--json                Emit the end-of-run report as one line of JSON on
stdout — same key contract and stream discipline as
`bale apply --json` (retry reruns the same pipeline):
'[bale] ' lines, prompts, and the human banners go to
stderr; stdout carries exactly the JSON line on the
reporting paths. Pair with --no-interact for scripted
retries.
